passage:
With exams a week away and rain drumming for days, Ganga cancelled her son Anand's evening cricket. "No playing until your marks improve," she said. Anand, nine, sat at the desk in their small house in Kozhikode, staring at sums. By Wednesday he was snapping at his little sister, kicking the chair legs and lying awake late into the night. His marks got worse, not better.
On Thursday the rain eased. Ganga watched him erase the same answer for the third time. "Go. One hour on the ground. Then sums."
Anand ran. He came back muddy and grinning, ate two helpings of rice, and finished his sums without a single fight. That night he was asleep early. Ganga put the cricket back on the timetable, every evening, exams or not.

qa.q: What did Ganga cancel?
qa.a: Ganga cancelled Anand's evening cricket.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling by Wednesday, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Anand felt restless and irritable; he snapped at his sister, kicked the chair legs and lay awake late.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Taking away play as a punishment made Anand's mood and marks worse; an hour on the ground brought back calm, sleep and focus.

qa.q: How did Ganga's view of the cricket change?
qa.a: Ganga first treated cricket as a reward to take away, then saw it as something Anand needs every evening.

grounding: Taking away a child's outdoor play worsens his mood, sleep and focus, while running and playing help him regulate his feelings.

passage:
When the housing society in Andheri banned games in the compound, eight-year-old Salma had nowhere to run after school. For a week she and her friend Hrithik stayed in their flats. Salma fought with her Ammi over bath time, cried over homework and tossed in bed for hours.
Then Ammi and Hrithik's father went to the society meeting. "Children need to run," Ammi said. "It's how they settle." The committee agreed to an evening play hour.
On the first evening, Salma and Hrithik played catch until they were breathless and red-cheeked. Salma came home, did her homework without a single tear, and fell asleep while Ammi was still reading to her.
"I feel nicer after running," Salma mumbled into her pillow. "Like my grumpy goes out through my feet."

qa.q: What did the committee agree to?
qa.a: The committee agreed to an evening play hour.

qa.q: How did Salma describe feeling after running?
qa.a: Salma felt nicer and calmer, saying the grumpy goes out through her feet.

qa.q: Why was Ammi's step at the society meeting wise?
qa.a: Ammi argued that children need to run to settle, and the play hour gave Salma a way to manage her feelings.

qa.q: How might the society committee see the play hour after hearing Ammi?
qa.a: The committee seem to see it as a fair balance between quiet in the compound and children's need to run.

grounding: A child who argues, cries and sleeps poorly without outdoor play settles far better once running is back in her day.

passage:
'Mummy, can I go to the park? Riya's there.'
'Not until your homework's done, Ayesha. And you were rude this morning, so no park today.'
'But I can't concentrate! My legs feel wiggly!'
'Then sit still until they stop.'
Ayesha slumped at the table, kicking the chair leg. Ten minutes later she'd written one line and snapped at her little brother twice.
Charu watched her. 'Ayesha, last Sunday after cricket, you did all your maths in twenty minutes, remember?'
'And I slept all night,' Ayesha mumbled.
Charu sighed. 'Okay. Taking the park away isn't working. Go for forty minutes. Then homework, and we'll talk about this morning later.'
Ayesha raced out. She came back pink-cheeked and calm, sat down and finished her homework without a single complaint.

qa.q: How long did Charu let Ayesha go to the park for?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling while stuck at the table?
qa.a: She was restless and cranky, with wiggly legs and snapping at her brother.

qa.q: What did Charu realise, and what did she change?
qa.a: That taking the park away was not working, so she let Ayesha play first and kept the talk about rudeness for later.

qa.q: How might Ayesha's little brother have been affected by her restlessness?
qa.a: He got snapped at twice, so he probably felt hurt or confused until she came back calmer.

grounding: Shows a child whose mood and focus improve after outdoor play, and a parent who stops using play as a reward to take away.

passage: The monsoon that year lasted forever. For two weeks the colony ground in Kochi was a lake, and my little sister Pooja and I were stuck inside. By the fourth day we were fighting about everything: the TV, the window seat, who breathed too loud. I couldn't fall asleep at night, and my homework took hours. Umma kept saying, 'What's wrong with you two?' Then the rain stopped on a Saturday. We ran out into the mud, played catch till our arms ached, raced each other round the building six times. That night I slept like a stone. On Monday I did my sums in half the time. Pooja and I didn't fight once. I'm Afreen, and I still remember thinking: oh, my body needed that.

qa.q: Where did Afreen and Pooja play when the rain stopped?
qa.a: Out in the mud, round the building.

qa.q: How did Afreen feel during the two weeks stuck inside?
qa.a: Afreen felt restless and irritable, fighting with Pooja and unable to sleep well.

qa.q: What does Afreen's story suggest parents could plan on rainy days?
qa.a: Finding ways for children to move and play, since being stuck indoors made both children cranky and restless.

qa.q: How might Umma have seen the change after the rain stopped?
qa.a: Umma was probably relieved to see the two children calm, sleeping and not fighting.

grounding: Shows a child who argues more and sleeps badly when kept indoors, and whose mood and sleep improve after running and playing outside.

passage:
PE department note to Class 5 teachers
For three weeks Chaitanya has been kept in during PE to finish unfinished classwork. I've noticed that on those days he is more restless, not less. He fidgets in the corridor, argues with classmates and, according to his mother, sleeps badly. On Thursday, by mistake, he came out and played football for the full period. Afterwards Vikas Sir from Class 5B told me Chaitanya finished his English worksheet quietly and even helped tidy up. I'd like to request that PE not be used as a punishment for any child. Running and play help children settle; taking them away seems to make things worse. Happy to discuss other consequences.
Mr Joseph, PE teacher

qa.q: How long has Chaitanya been kept in during PE?
qa.a: For three weeks.

qa.q: What might Chaitanya be feeling on days he misses PE?
qa.a: He seems restless and cranky, fidgeting and arguing with classmates.

qa.q: What did Mr Joseph suggest instead of keeping children in?
qa.a: That PE should not be used as punishment, and that other consequences be discussed.

qa.q: How did Vikas Sir see Chaitanya after the football period?
qa.a: Vikas Sir saw a calmer boy who finished his worksheet quietly and helped tidy up.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing that a child kept from play is more restless and sleeps worse, and arguing that physical play is part of how children regulate feelings.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today was a GOOD day. It rained all week and we were stuck indoors, and I was so grumpy I fought with Imran over the TV remote three times. Last night I couldn't even sleep properly. Today the sun came out and Ammi sent us to the park. Imran and I raced to the big tree ten times, played catch and rolled down the grassy slope till we were dizzy. When we came home I did all my maths without a single fight. Ammi said, 'See what running does?' Even Imran was nice. Tomorrow Ms Pinto wants to keep us in at games time to finish our project. I'm going to ask her if we can finish it after school instead.
Reena

qa.q: How many times did Reena and Imran race to the big tree?
qa.a: Ten times.

qa.q: How did Reena feel after the week stuck indoors?
qa.a: Reena felt grumpy and restless, fighting with Imran and sleeping badly.

qa.q: Why is it sensible for Reena to ask Ms Pinto to keep games time?
qa.a: Physical play helps Reena's mood and focus, so taking it away could make work and behaviour worse, not better.

qa.q: How might Ammi see the change after the park?
qa.a: Ammi likely felt pleased and relieved, seeing running bring back peace and focus.

grounding: A child who runs and plays outdoors sleeps and behaves better, and physical play is part of how children regulate feelings.
